Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I am sure that the hon. member would not want to mislead the House. The motion does not say that the report should be implemented at this time or any other time. The motion very specifically says:
-consider the advisability of implementing-
How can a government possibly go against considering the advisability of implementing its own report? The motion says nothing about implementing the report at this time, just about considering it. I am sure that the hon. member would not want to mislead the House.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS SUGGESTING CONSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I will speak against the advisability of implementing the report, Mr. Speaker. There are a number of points which are consistently made when this topic is discussed in the House of Commons and which I feel should be dealt with.
The hon. member for the Western Arctic, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), and occasionally others in the party opposite, referred to the state of colonialism that exists in the north. The hon. member for Western Arctic was a little more moderate-1 believe he said quasi colonialism.
The leader of the Conservative party in the Yukon, Mr. Pearson, who for a short period was designated by the former minister of indian affairs and northern development as premier, used the term first-class and second-class citizen. Yukoners apparently are not first class citizens, and the same
July 21, 1980

argument, presumably, would apply to people living in the Northwest Territories. Let us examine this for a minute, Mr. Speaker.
1 would ask the forgiveness of the hon. member for the Western Arctic for my continual reference to the Yukon, but I use the Yukon argument because the Northwest Territories is perhaps a few years behind in constitutional development, but not too many years, so the arguments which apply to the Yukon may apply, two or three years ahead, to the Northwest Territories.
Let us look at the argument that people in those two territories are somehow second-class citizens and are being colonized by the rest of the country. The total population of the Yukon, 23,000, and of the Northwest Territories, 45,000, represents percentages of the Canadian total which do not stand up to comparisons between the situation when Manitoba entered confederation and the situation today, vis-a-vis the total population. The Yukon's percentage of the total population is less than one-tenth of 1 per cent of our total. When Manitoba entered confederation, 1 believe the province's percentage of the Canadian total was around 1 per cent, ten times higher. Yet the argument is made that the comparison with Manitoba, which had something like 25,000 people when it became a province, favours the immediate move for the Yukon, and later the Northwest Territories, toward provincial status. That is not the case; things have changed, Mr. Speaker.
When Manitoba entered confederation, her population was about to explode. That is not going to happen in the Yukon unless, of course, the kind of thing occurs that is being proposed by certain politicians there who would like an immediate move toward provincial status, in that case, a completely artificial situation would occur. In order to justify provincial status there would be an artificial stimulation of a population move into the Yukon.
This is where we come to the root of the quandary about development in the north. The people who want development per se are usually those with the most political clout who can make the most political noise. Through chambers of commerce and businessmen's associations, they are able to exercise pressure on politicians in the north for an immediate move toward provincial status. They are primarily interested in all the business activity that is anticipated if they could somehow achieve control via the provincehood vehicle.
That is a very dangerous concept indeed from the point of view of the native people. I think the hon. member who comes from the eastern Arctic expressed this in the hesitation he showed in embracing the idea of provincial status. In effect it would mean that with the province in full control of immigration and stimulating economic development in a way that would not necessarily make economic good sense but would bring people in to justify the apparatus being set up, native people would be overrun by a larger population coming in from the south. This is a demographic fear which is well based and well justified, in my view. This is probably the most basic reason why there should be no movement toward provincehood now in the Yukon or in the Northwest Territories.
Northwest Territories
There are a host of other reasons why we should move slowly in the direction which, for a time last year, seemed to be toward creating a province within the next three years. The then prime minister indicated that he intended to create a province in the Yukon before the end of his first term in office. Fortunately for everyone in Canada, that did not happen. I say "fortunately" because when we are talking about the north we are talking about something which, in the minds of a lot of people in the country, helps tie Canada together.
There is a common heritage which we all share in the north. We share it on the land mass in the north and we share it on the offshore areas of the north. No one in this House would suggest that northerners should not have first call on the resources of the north, the extent of which we do not yet know. As far as I am concerned, they should have first call on them in order to assure themselves of a standard of living second to none. Beyond that, however, I think the rest of Canada should participate in whatever riches are found there.
Until now-and for the foreseeable future-the Canadian taxpayer has been footing a major portion of the bill. We pay 60 per cent of the public service costs in the Yukon and a higher percentage for the Northwest Territories. All Canadians have made these contributions and in fairness, over the long run, we should expect a return.
The path for constitutional evolution should not necessarily be provincehood, it seems to me. It may be provincehood, but we should not bind ourselves to that single objective.
From my experience and through talking to northerners over the years, 1 believe that the one idea that keeps coming back is, "Let's get rid of that federal red tape." 1 quite agree. If we could somehow rid the northerners of their impression that they are always tied up in federal tape, we could solve a lot of problems. I would point out as well that politicians in the two northern territories have become as adept as separatist politicians in Quebec at pointing out deficiencies in the federal government. In addition, they point out how in some instances, where there are perfectly normal, legitimate reasons for slowness in achieving results, the federal government is somehow totally to blame because of this insensitive, slow, lethargic public service which looks after relations between the people there and the government here in Ottawa. They point out distances and bring all these reasons together and point out that somehow the system is not working.
We should be aiming for a solution in the north which could be used as a model for future constitutional developments in the rest of Canada. Let us keep our minds open. Fortunately, the report does not specify a single constitutional objective. I would hope that all members of this House could take a new look at just where we are heading in the north. 1 feel there are other solutions which will help the people in the north better than anything that has been proposed so far and yet will preserve this kind of cement which the common heritage represents for all of us as part of Canada.

speechtext: When the debate on the motion was interrupted at five o'clock, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, now that we have had the opportunity of dining, the NDP will go up to the dining room to get a few more members into the House to make sure that they have ten here so that any motion which might be contrary to their interests of having a full meal can be overcome.
1 want to carry on my remarks. Before the adjournment for the dinner hour, 1 had the opportunity to consider the position vis-a-vis the record of this government on energy matters as a whole, about which we should be concerned.
I am glad the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) is here to listen to this because rarely does he have an opportunity of hearing good, simple, common sense. He should stay in the House more regularly where he will have the opportunity to hear these contributions. Then he would not be in the position to delay and waste the time of the House as he now does.
Before the dinner adjournment, I stated that it was a rather abysmal record with respect to this government in terms of energy policy. We have had virtually no initiatives at all respecting our energy policy, and no legislation. None of the
initiatives mentioned in the Speech from the Throne have been brought forward.
It is amazing that we now have a situation where, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) so often puts it, the natural allies of the government, the New Democrats, are making a big ruckus so that it will appear they have a main difference in terms of policy. We know that the Liberal government, for all intents and purposes, over the course of the administration of this Prime Minister, has been kept in office by the very same NDP. Therefore, it ill behooves them to stand up now and pretend they are speaking on behalf of the interests of Canadians when they themselves kept the Liberals in power over the past 12 years by constantly voting, particularly in minority situations, to keep them in power. The people of Canada will reflect on this during the adjournment debate. It will allow them to think about whether there is a trace, or a touch, of hypocrisy in what the NDP are doing in terms of this debate.
What concerns me is that this very government, supported by the NDP, has made no progress at all in terms of energy policy. What is even more distressing and disturbing is the fact that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), in terms of our energy policy and domestic oil pricing, left the whole issue until a couple of weeks or months before the expiration of existing arrangements in Canada. In fact, we have now passed the expiration date on June 30 and are faced with an extension, which has been agreed to by the producing provinces and the federal government, until the end of July.
One would have expected all sorts of activity during the month of July in which negotiations on a new arrangement would have been carried on, but no, we are going to adjourn this House. The meeting of the Prime Minister and Mr. Lougheed will not take place until July 24, a mere six days before the conclusion of the extension period. Many people in Canada do not fully understand the implications of the federal government and the producing provinces not arriving at an agreement. There are certain central issues preoccupying the government in terms of this negotiation.
The central issue, in my view, is the whole question of revenue sharing and the recycling of funds that has been and will continue to flow to the producing provinces. They like to concentrate their attention on the province of Alberta because it is by far the largest producer of oil in this country. We have to look at what is going on in this negotiation.
From my reading of the situation and observing it, unfortunately from the sidelines now, the parties are very far apart in terms of an agreement. The federal government is trying to achieve some process by which there will be a bigger take on the part of the federal government with regard to revenues on oil. There are some suggestions that that is what the federal government is trying to do in this connection. They are talking about a number of prospects through their blended oil price, blending some combination of old and new oil. Through this processing, the Oil Import Compensation Act, to equalize the cost of imported fuel, will continually be reduced through some sort of charge to the refineries. This is something the
July 21, 1980

federal government is considering with respect to its negotiations with the producing provinces.
1 am concerned about the prospect of no agreement having been reached by the end of this month. Unless there is an awful lot of change in position, there is a very distinct possibility that this will take place over a very short period of time. We face the potential prospect of there being no agreement between the federal and provincial governments.
It is very easy to consider different scenarios as to what might transpire if an agreement is not reached. I suppose everyone can make his own scenario, but there are different possibilities we should consider. Conceivably we could stay here if the members of the New Democratic Party decide to speak indefinitely over the course of the summer and bore everybody to death. There are some possible scenarios, and these would involve either the federal government or the provincial governments taking some initiatives with respect to the important question of oil pricing.
One scenario could be that, if there is no agreement, the federal government will decide unilaterally to announce its own energy policy, including a set of oil prices. Let us assume that if the federal government takes that initiative, the province of Alberta, being the largest producer of oil in our country, could either follow those prices or take its own initiative, with instructions to the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission to offer Alberta oil at a particular price set by it.
Conceivably the price could be higher than the one suggested by the federal government because the federal government, 1 suppose, is interested in carrying out its election promise of low prices or cheap energy for Canadians. The federal government price would be imposed under the provisions of the Petroleum Administration Act, part II, and if there were this conflict, another distinct possibility could be a very serious confrontation in the courts. There could be a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to determine the constitutionality of pricing on the part of the federal government as opposed to the provincial governments, and to determine which should prevail in constitutional terms.
Another possibility is that the province of Alberta could consider using as its weapon the provisions of the Mines and Minerals Amendments Act of 1980 to limit the movement of crude oil out of Alberta. A question could arise as to whether that would be sustainable as being within the jurisdiction of the provincial government to take that option. However, the consequences would be very serious, whether we are talking in terms of conserving a resource which is a depleting resource or using this as a vehicle for strife with the federal government.
Another possibility might be that the Alberta government might consider taking steps with respect to provincial Crown leases or royalty land and simply not allowing any oil to be lifted from royalty land or Crown land. In any event, this could lead to very long, protracted and difficult legal action which would have serious consequences for our country.
Summer Recess
In addition to that there is the whole question of whether we in Canada would become more and more reliant on offshore oil. That matter would very quickly come to the forefront because of the uncertainty caused by lack of agreement and because of the possibility of action taken by producing provinces with respect to oil in their jurisdictions, and there is no doubt that if this takes place, there would be two consequences. One would be increased reliance on offshore imports, which would create serious economic consequences for our country, especially in view of the international price and the fact that the oil import compensation program is now in such a horrible deficit position. The second consequence would be the implementation of the Energy Supplies Emergency Act passed in 1979, and we in Canada would be faced with the propect of allocation and presumably rationing of petroleum products.
These could be some of the consequences of the drift and the almost cavalier attitude the federal government has taken in energy negotiations. We should be greatly concerned, as we participate in this adjournment debate, about what is going to transpire, whether or not the adjournment will be until October next. In light of the possibility of there being no agreement, there is the prospect of this kind of confrontation. Notwithstanding the New Democratic Party, we could be back here, if there is no agreement, sooner than we think and sooner than anticipated by this motion.
I am giving the House a report card, so to speak, on this government's record in terms of energy policy. Its record is dismal. There has been literally no action or initiatives taken since this government came to power. We face a very serious prospect of a breakdown in terms of agreement between the federal and provincial governments. The negotiation of an agreement has been left, not to the eleventh hour but to the thirteenth hour. An agreement is past due already.
In a non-partisan and serious way I question the effectiveness of the government, and 1 question very seriously the New Democratic Party for its continued support of the Liberal government over a long period of time. I know there are arguments and a lot of shouting, but marital breakdown is always very distressing.
With the Liberal party and the New Democratic Party fighting as they are, I want to close my remarks by telling a story told by a person who has been quoted over and over again by speakers from the New Democratic Party. I refer to the Hon. T. C. Douglas. Mr. Douglas is now one of the corporate boardroom bums referred to by the New Democratic Party. It will be interesting to see whether members of the NDP will take advice from Mr. Douglas now as they have in the past. He is a member of the board of directors of Husky Oil. He is with all the bigwigs of the oil industry. He sits with Husky Oil directors and others.

Mr. Speaker, I would not want to leave the wrong impression. I did not refuse the hon. member the right to proceed. I was just shaking my head at the pitiful effort he put forward. I could not imagine wanting to inflict any more of that on the House.
I have been listening with interest to the speakers who have preceded me. 1 listened to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) with considerable interest, hoping to grasp or to hear some indication of what the Liberal party really believed. I listened to the hon. member for Saskatchewan West- Saskatoon West-
Saskatchewan is the province; Saskatoon is the city.

I realize that. I listened to the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) with interest because he seemed for one reason or another to want to address himself more to the NDP than to the issue. As I listened to him and tried to compare what he was saying with what has been said by other Conservative members over the course of the last week, or perhaps week and a half, with regard to energy policy and this particular problem of the pre-build, I came to the conclusion, in the words of a close colleague of mine, that the Conservative party, on this issue at least, has more positions than Masters and Johnson.
Bill Davis used that line three weeks ago on you guys.

It is a shame that we have not really addressed this very crucial problem. This is an important day in the history of Canada. We are debating an issue which could well decide the economic future of the country. We are talking about whether or not this country will be self-sufficient in energy, with energy available from coast to coast in years to come. We are talking about the single most valuable resource any country can have. We are very privileged as a country because we have energy in various forms and in sufficient quantities to allow us to be self-sufficient. We have energy which very few industrialized countries in the world have available to them, we have the capacity right in this country to develop an economy, job opportunities and a quality of life second to none. Yet, the government makes a decision which allows some of that very valuable energy, which no doubt we will need some day in the future, to be exported out of the country to the United States without any consideration for how it will be replaced, what it will cost to replace it, or for the fact that future generations will require that energy for their needs. That is what the issue is all about today, and that is what we should be talking about.
I thought for a while that the Liberal party understood the issue. I listened with interest to the comments made by Liberals over the course of the last year. 1 read with interest what was said by the Liberal party during the debates in the House of Commons prior to the last election and on the hustings during the last election. 1 read with interest the comments of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). Here is a nationalist if ever I saw one, or at least so he says. As reported in Hansard of December 12, 1979, he said:
The Conservative answer to our balance of payments problem is to encourage more exports of unprocessed non-renewable raw material. This, in fact, is what their decision to allow larger exports of natural gas really means. Rather than use it to build up and expand our petrochemical industry, rather than use it as a substitute for imported oil, Conservatives have agreed to export it, and they have done so without getting any commitment that American gas will be available later for Canada on a swap basis at the same price.
He then went on to say:
They have done so without getting any commitment in return from the United States for greater access for our manufactured goods. The Conservatives have allowed these exports, without getting any final commitment on the building of the northern gas pipeline. They do not have any final commitment from the gas producers that they will finance and ensure the building of a natural gas pipeline to Atlantic Canada. Instead, through this budget, Canadians are being asked to pay higher fuel prices and higher taxes under the guise of helping Canada reach energy self-sufficiency.
He went on to say:
But to the extent any of this money is used to find new oil and new natural gas, I ask the House what assurance Canadians have from the Conservative government that any new reserves found at the expense of Canadian taxpayers, middle and lower-income Canadians, will not simply be exported to the United States.
This is happening with much of the reserves of natural gas found in recent years in Canada, natural gas reserves found with money put up by Canadian taxpayers through higher prices and tax expenditures. That was the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce speaking in the budget debate. When one reads that, one says to oneself, "Now, there is a man who knows what the problem is". My colleague sitting beside me said under his breath, "What a phony". I wish he would say it louder.
What a phony.
Thank you. It is quite clear to everyone exactly what that was. Of course it was not only the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He is not the only phony on the Liberal benches.
Do not forget the Tories.

We will get to the Tories. I should like to refer to the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He said before the Standing Committee on Northern Pipelines on March 20, 1979:
It is the policy of this government that we will insist upon a guarantee that the total line be built, that the financial arrangements for the building of the entire line be in place before we give the green light for going ahead with the pre-build.
That was the Minister of Finance speaking. There was another phony, if I ever heard one. Then there was the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde),
July 21, 1980

kindly soul that he is, speaking on behalf of Canadians and looking after our best interests, so to speak. As reported in the record of the House of Commons for the fall of 1979, he said:
In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all, an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline. Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered, particularly the financing guarantees, before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.
Well, we have the phony Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the phonier Minister of Finance, and now we have this kindly gent who poses as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and tries to tell us that, all of a sudden, as if by some magical means, a new light has dawned and he sees a new truth. Now he is really speaking on behalf of the Liberal party and in the best interests of Canadians. What kind of nonsense is this? What kind of nonsense are we faced with? We are faced with a bankrupt political party which sells out the country, a political party which turns around and allows development to take place which in fact will cause untold hardship in years to come. We are faced with a political party which does not protect the interests of Canadians, a political party which says one thing that suits it one day and an entirely different thing another day.
And your party supported them last December.

It does not even marginally alter its position, but it changes 180 degrees every time. One has to wonder about this political party; in office and out of office they are a very strange bunch.
Not only did they say those things while they debated in the House of Commons, not only did they put these positions forward in an attempt to embarrass the easily embarrassed Conservative party, but then they went out on to the hustings and told Canadians that they would put in place an energy policy which would work in the best interests of Canadians.
On January 25, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke in Halifax, he said quite clearly that the Liberal party would put in place an energy policy that met all the requirements which guaranteed Canadians access to their resources, which would make available to Canadians the energy resources they needed at a price they could afford, that we would see the kind of energy policy coming from them, if they were re-elected, which would satisfy the needs of Canada now and into the future. For example, they said that there would be a natural gas pipeline to ensure access by all Canadians to their resources. The Liberals would take immediate action to begin negotiations for the construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritimes. Initially it would carry natural gas east, but when the maritime supplies were ready, the pipeline would be like a natural gas railroad with a return delivery facility as well.
Double tracking.

Perhaps he was talking about double tracking. He went on to say that the Liberals would ensure that
Summer Recess
Canada's energy sector became more Canadian-owned and controlled. Also he said that industry would be developed close to energy sources, so that producing areas in the west and elsewhere would have first chance at processing the resources. Where will it be developed? Will it be in the southern United States? Is that the government's policy? The Liberal party was stumping around the country trying to gain support during the last election campaign. When the Conservative party approved of 3.75 trillion cubic feet of natural gas being sold to the United States, on January 9 the Prime Minister, who was then leader of the opposition, said:	.
By just approving that export without conditions, it lost another great chance for our industrial development.
He was referring to the Conservative government. Hon. members are bound to ask themselves: What is it about this political party? What are the people supposed to believe about this political party? This Liberal party, when out of office, says anything it can to get into office and when it is in office, does anything it can to get rid of the resources of Canada. 1 had a colleague in the legislature and he sometimes used a phrase which 1 shall repeat-no doubt members have heard it before. He used to say that putting the Liberals in charge of resources was like putting Dracula in charge of a blood bank.
There are problems attached to the course the government is about to embark upon and there are risks which Liberal supporters have failed to recognize. I watched with a sick feeling as Liberals leaped to support the minister of energy as he made his statement the other evening. 1 watched as they euphorically applauded the sell-out of our resources, the building of the pipeline from resources we are going to need, to provide for the greed of the United States. I watched it happening. I said to myself: surely they do not understand the position; surely they do not have the evidence before them; they cannot know what it is all about or they must be very easily led. Accordingly, I thought I would put on record tonight some of the reasons for which I believe that this proposal is bad for Canada now and will be bad for the nation in the future.
To begin with, it has been said that the rate at which natural gas is being discovered, not only here in Canada but in the lower 48 states and in the Gulf of Mexico, makes it quite possible, if not quite probable, that given the high cost of bringing gas from Alaska to the market the project will not be pursued-that at some point in time there will be more readily-available and cheaper gas for exploitation by the United States, not only in that country but here, where they are getting access to our supplies of natural gas. So there is no reason for them to spend many billions of dollars pursuing an expensive source of energy after we have given them free access, as it were, to cheaper energy sources.
In addition, there is no question that once we have committed ourselves to the pre-build, Canadians will have to finance the entire operation by continuing to export the natural gas which belongs to us for far beyond the short term envisaged by

the present decision. Further, there is no question but that the history of the last decade is repeating itself. The same Liberal government as we see there today made all kinds of grand predictions in the past about the availability of oil and then proceeded to sell it off as quickly as they could at a cheap price until we were forced to go into the marketplace and buy back what we needed. At that point, of course, the price was way out of proportion to the cost of production.
1 suggest the same thing is about to happen again in the case of natural gas. The Liberal party is certainly consistent in this regard. We shall find ourselves in the position of having to buy natural gas from other sources in the not too distant future and in so doing we shall be paying ten or 20 times what we might have paid had we held on to our own supplies.
Hear, hear!

The minister says there is a surplus of natural gas. Mr. Speaker, there might be a surplus of commodities which can rot; there might even be a surplus of products which can go out of date. But there can be no surplus of energy. We do not even know at this point what kind of economic development will take place in Canada in the future. Bear in mind that so far we have been unable to provide natural gas for the people in our own country who so desperately need it. We are being forced today to pay something like $3.6 billion to subsidize the purchase of oil from offshore though we could have used our own natural gas to replace expensive foreign oil. Until such time as we have an industrial strategy in place and until such time as gas is available to people all across this country, bringing them energy at a price they can afford, there is no one in this government or in the National Energy Board who can prove to me that there is in fact a surplus.
Hear, hear!
There is no surplus.
You have to prove it.

I do not have to prove it. It is as plain as the nose on your face. We do not have a national energy policy. The Liberal government has no idea how they are going to integrate our energy resources, no idea how they will be used. They do not know what proportion of our energy needs will be met by oil or what proportion will be met by gas or what proportion will be met by electricity or what proportion will be met by coal, not to mention new resources. Until such time as an energy policy is in place, how can we determine that there is a surplus of one of the components? What the government is doing, supported by its inadequate backbenchers, is this: it is rushing ahead to sell off our gas reserves for a quick buck today without any consideration for the cost of replacement or for the needs of people in the future.
How can you say that without smiling?

Anyone looking at this so-called energy policy would have to agree that the decision to go ahead with the pre-build is an ad hoc decision based on nothing of any
consequence, based on the creation of a certain number of short-term jobs. Mr. Speaker, if we were to embark on providing a means of moving the gas from the existing natural gas fields to the east and the west coasts, we would be able to provide even more short-term jobs but, in addition, we would be able to set up an infrastructure which would allow us to encourage the industrial and economic development needed to bring about long-term jobs for Canadians. And that should be the goal of any government in office these days.
Hear, hear!
1 am sure Liberal backbenchers are impressed enough now by the arguments-

speechtext: Order. It is difficult to hear in the chamber if hon. members interrupt.
Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry that you cannot hear me. I am trying to speak directly to you, and if the Liberal backbenchers would sit quietly, 1 could have you listen.
Just like you did last week.

You are insulting the Speaker. He wants to hear. Since they do not care, Mr. Speaker, I shall speak to you. Since it is quite obvious that the Liberal party does not give a damn about Canada, you and I will talk about it. There are certain facts about the pipeline which cannot be overlooked. To begin with, we all understand that the total cost of the project will be in excess of $20 billion, perhaps even $30 billion or $40 billion, before it ever gets under way, if it ever gets under way. Over 80 per cent of that cost will be borrowed by the principals from normal lending sources.
This is the largest single financial investment which has ever been undertaken in the private sector. It is clear that the people or institutions lending the money will demand explicit and comprehensive assurances. They will want to have guarantees that their loans will be paid with interest according to a pre-arranged schedule.
Just like Chrysler.
The simple fact is that the Alaska highway pipeline sponsors cannot provide those guarantees because the pipeline costs considerably exceed their assets.
Give us a figure.
The figure at the moment is about $30 billion and the total assets of the sponsors do not come close to half of that.

You're guessing.
July 21, 1980

The pipeline will be financed on the strength of the transmission of gas through the pipeline. Because there are risks that the pipeline might not generate sufficient revenues to cover the debt interest and the generated costs, institutional lenders will demand guarantees.
The guarantees will have to be provided by government at one level or another. There is the serious risk of non-completion of the pipeline. That becomes clearer with every passing day. There is the serious risk, and it is almost a guarantee, of cost overruns on a project of this size. There is of course the interruption or, if you will, the reduction of the service. A Wall Street investment banker, quoted in Energy Daily of November 4, 1977 said:
Remember, this is the largest single project ever undertaken by anybody in private industry. For every institution that takes part in it, it will be the largest investment they ever made in anything. No one will move an inch-
No one will sign, no one will put out a penny, no one will sign a document until the guarantees are in place for every single step of the project through to its completion. When one stops to think about it, one says to oneself, "The guarantees, obviously, must come from government". They must come primarily from the federal government of the United States because it is, after all, a pipeline for the United States to bring gas from Alaska to the lower 48 states. That is what the pipeline is all about. Therefore, the United States must find a way to guarantee the financing.
The U.S. department of the treasury has maintained since 1975 that the pipelines' beneficiaries-Prudhoe Bay, Exxon, Sohio, the state of Alaska, the natural gas transmission industry-which, most notably, includes Northwest Pipeline in the U.S. and Foothills in Canada-would have to provide the guarantees required by lenders. In a report prepared for the Alaska state legislature by Dr. Arlon Tussing and released in April, 1979, the following conclusion was drawn:
The Alaska highway gas pipeline cannot be financed and built unless the United States government guarantees at least part of the project debt.
However, Northwest Pipeline Company of the U.S. will find it difficult obtaining financial guarantees from the U.S. government. The report of the U.S. Senate energy committee accompanying the congressional resolution endorsing President Carter's pipeline decision in October, 1977, stated:
It is essential for the project sponsors to proceed with their financial arrangements as promptly as possible. The state of Alaska, the producers, and most of all, the project sponsors should bear in mind that the door to the federal treasury has not been left open to them-
That is the federal treasury of the United States. But much more persuasive, from my point of view, than the rather innocuous self-serving letter put forward by the Prime Minister, is the fact that President Carter in 1977, in his decision and report to Congress on the Alaska natural gas transportation system, rejected government guarantees on the following grounds: one, serious questions of equity result from the transfer of risks to taxpayers, many of whom are not gas consumers and will not receive additional gas supplies as the result of the Alaska project; two, federal financial support substitutes the government for private lenders in the critical risk assessment function; three, the incentive for an efficient
Summer Recess
management of the project is reduced; and four, the government is placed in conflicting roles as guarantor and as regulator of the project.
President Carter made it clear that on these grounds he would not recommend that the federal government of the United States embark on many guarantees or in any direct way become involved in the financing of the Alaska Highway pipeline. When one stops and weighs that against that quite inadequate document produced in the House last Thursday-
Unsigned.

-unsigned and which was supposed to sell us on the commitment of the President of the United States over and against a carefully thought out position put before his own legislators, 1 think, if I were to make the judgment, I would believe his original statement, and I believe that the government should believe it as well.
One must also bear in mind that even if the Northwest Pipeline approaches institutional investors with a financial package before the end of 1980, with a presidential election this year Congress will likely not address the question of government guarantees until at least 1981. This pushes the completion back to 1986 at the earliest, and that is already one year later than we heard on Thursday.
If 1 were to make judgments about the intention of the U.S. government to do something which we must have if this project is to be successful, 1 would have to come to the conclusion that, on a number of very valid grounds backed up by their own statements, there is no likelihood that the United States will be able to proceed with the development of the pipeline in its entirety, that they will syphon off what they can get from us at the lowest possible price, that we will receive nothing in return other than today's dollar value and that we will inevitably have to purchase gas to replace that gas, for which we will have to pay the price of the day, and that may be five years, six years or ten years from today. That, my friends, constitutes a rip-off of Canadian resources.
Hear, hear!

We ought to look at what others are saying. We have looked at what the Liberals have said when out of office, when in office, at the flip-flop, the fact that you cannot trust the Liberal government, that you never know where they are coming from or what they will do. We have looked at the sell-out of our oil resources in the early seventies when they were well warned that the result would be higher costs for Canadians. We have looked at the potential of providing at least an equal number of jobs for Canadians, and of building an east-west facility rather than a north-south facility. We have suggested that in the best economic interests of the country and its future, and the need to provide energy at the lowest possible cost for the use of Canadians, we should be building an east-west pipeline rather than a north-south pipeline.
We have suggested that when in 1978 a bill was passed by this Parliament to approve the northern Alaska highway pipeline, it was intended to be a transmission line from Alaska to the United States and that this decision does not conform with that legislation. We have pointed out, I think, that the possibilities of getting this pipeline completed are slim if they exist at all. It is clear that the government in the United States recognizes all the pitfalls I have set out and that the President of the United States has quite clearly set out for his own Congress the fact that they cannot possibly undertake the financing of the pipeline because of a number of factors which I have enumerated.
It is therefore clear to me, and I now suggest to many Canadians, that the decision being taken by the Liberal government today is not in the best interests of Canada. It is that simple, Mr. Speaker. It is that simple.
What do you suggest, then?

I think, instead of talking, if the hon. member had listened, he would have heard. Let me tell him that the learned commentators of the media have set out some very clear positions on this. Almost without exception editors across this country have said that the government's decision is wrongheaded; that the government's decision, if it has to be taken at all, should not be taken now-that it should be delayed and there should be an opportunity for careful review. They have said that if by any chance the decision turns out to be in the best interest of Canada, this should be clear to everyone before the project is proceeded with.
On every open line program, the overwhelming majority of people who have phoned in have made it clear that they want to develop their own resources for their own needs and for the future. There is something wrong with a government that does not listen to anyone.
There is something wrong with your party.

Let me address myself to the mouthy member in the back row. There is an opportunity to do useful things for this country. To begin with, the government should put an end to this now. They should say that the decision was hasty-that they are going to reconsider and make sure that whatever is about to be undertaken is stopped.
Hear, hear!

Second, the government should make a decision today to build a pipeline from the natural gas fields in Alberta, British Columbia and other parts of the west, to both Vancouver Island and the maritimes. That would provide the shortterm jobs everyone says we must have. That would be a concrete decision and would go toward meeting the third goal.
The third goal would be a move toward reducing the need for importing oil to the east coast, a considerable financial burden to the Canadian public, and would enable us to undertake a replacement program which would allow this government and this country to transfer its dependence from offshore oil to natural gas.
The fourth point is that with those things in place it would be possible to start a concerted effort for economic development across the country because we would have an assured supply of energy from coast to coast at a price that we in Canada could regulate. We would have an assured supply of energy coast to coast that would guarantee that our industry could, if we so desired, be more competitive-could be competitive with anyone in the world.
We should be following the example of other oil producers and other energy producers of using our energy and oil to develop the country where we have jurisdiction so that the people of Canada can benefit.
That is the kind of program that I suggest this government should follow. Unfortunately, the government does not appear to have what it takes to make the tough decisions. It is always easy to turn around and give things away-to go for the buck right now, no matter what the end cost will be. That is what this government has done every year it has been in office. That is why this government will, in historical perspective, stand indicted for the moves taken over the last few days.
They will go down in history known for the sell-out of our natural resources.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party does not understand. There was a delay in the proposed pipeline to move natural gas from Alaska to the United States through Canada. There was a delay in the original design of this project for certain reasons that are entirely outside the control of the Government of Canada and of the Canadian company responsible for construction within Canada.
And the fact is, Mr. Speaker, that if the government had not gone ahead with the approval of that section of the pipeline called the pre-build, those delays would have meant that Foothills (Yukon) would have found it impossible in the present circumstances to meet the requirements to set up the financing of the line within Canada unless the Government of Canada approved that construction. Once the Canadian energy agency said there was a surplus of natural gas in Canada, the export of that natural gas meant more money for the Alberta producers who are now in a situation where they have shut-in gas that is capped; that gas cannot be exported, so this decision allows the export of more natural gas, but it also allows Foothills Pipelines to generate revenues and pay not only for the pre-build now but the whole section of the pipeline that will be on Canadian territory. And without that decision at this moment, Mr. Speaker, we were running the risk that this project, at least as far as the Canadian section is concerned, might never take place, but the NDP were prepared to run that risk.
Mr. Speaker, the surplus of natural gas in Canada as indicated not by just anybody, not simply by Liberal members, not simply by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), but by the National Energy Board which made an appropriate study, the competent authority in Canada on energy-that agency said we now had in Canada a surplus of about 4.5 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
Mr. Speaker, the NDP say we are selling out Canada. What are the facts, Mr. Speaker? 1 checked how much surplus natural gas Canada has and here are the figures obtained from the National Energy Board. The export commitment for the pre-build, which was authorized last week and which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced in the House last week, will mean 2.3 trillion cubic feet of natural gas between 1980 and 1987. At the present time, up to 1980, the total gas export commitments allowed in Canada amount
July 21, 1980

to 14.5 trillion cubic feet. You will note that we are only talking here about 2.3 trillion, but the total up to 1980 amounts to 14.5 trillion cubic feet.
Canadian needs during the next decade will amount to 21 trillion cubic feet. In other words, total requirements between 1980 and 1990, that is for export and for Canadian needs, will be 35.5. trillion cubic feet. At the present time, western gas reserves amount to 71.8 trillion cubic feet. NDP members are confused by the facts, and because this time the facts are the opposite of what they would like, they are trying to hide them. Why does he not come up with the facts to show that the National Energy Board has found that we will be short of natural gas in the future? He does not give them, not at all.

I hear the hon. member for Broadview-Green-wood interjecting. He will speak in this debate. He can give us the facts.

When the National Energy Board approves an application for the export of gas, they use three tests to determine whether Canadian requirements can be met by current reserves and if the export should be approved.
I gave the absolute figures a while ago regarding what the reserves are, what the potential reserves are and what the domestic requirements would be in the next decade. The first test is the current deliverability test. It is based on the level of deliveries possible each year from established reserves. For there to be a surplus, the deliverability from these reserves has to be able to meet annual Canadian requirements plus current-

July 21, 1980
Summer Recess
ly authorized exports for a minimum period. This period is five years.
The second test is the current reserves test. This test compares the inventory of established reserves with 25 times the first year's Canadian demand, plus currently authorized exports. That is the second test before exports are approved.
The third test is the future deliverability test. It is based on the level of deliveries possible each year from established reserves and from estimated future additions to these reserves. Deliverability from these reserves has to be able to meet forecast annual Canadian requirements plus currently authorized exports for some ten years into the future. The most stringent of the three tests governs the amount of gas declared surplus.
Those are the facts. That is how the National Energy Board arrives at decisions.
Who provides the figures?

If the NDP wants to provide facts to the National Energy Board, all its members have to do is to go to the NEB and produce the facts. If the NDP has facts to show that this is not correct and that the numbers the NEB has found to be surplus are incorrect, why do its members just stand up in the House and make dogmatic speeches? My friend does not have the facts.
You have nothing.
You guys are stupid.

Canadians will always have priority with regard to access to their own gas. That is because, under section 83 of the National Energy Board Act, gas cannot be declared surplus until Canadian needs are met. In addition, new exports will stimulate drilling activity, and more gas will be found.

What about oil?

The hon. member comes back to oil. He loses the debate on gas, so he comes back to oil. If he wants to raise a question about oil, he can do that, and I will answer him, but today 1 am talking about gas.
I have all sorts of information I could put into the record to prove that the NDP just does not have the facts, but let us look at the decision and the benefits this decision will bring to Canada. The total and indirect employment generated by the
entire $8.4 billion pipeline project in Canada is estimated at 350,000 man-years.
Baloney.

The hon. member says "baloney". He wants workers to eat just bologna because he does not want the pre-build.
There will be capital expenditures of $1.6 billion for prebuilding the western and eastern legs, and gas production, conditioning and gathering systems at a cost of $935 million are estimated by the company to create 150,000 man-years of employment directly and indirectly. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain worries about the future. He does not worry about the workers of STELCO in the city of Hamilton. This is going to create 12,000 man-years of employment.
Not in Hamilton.

1 am a member of Parliament from a high unemployment area in the country. I do not understand how a member from prosperous Hamilton could reject 12,000 man-years of employment. It baffles me.
The export sales revenue from this project will be $17 billion. The change in the gross national product of Canada in 1980 will be .2 per cent. By 1987 it will be .5 per cent. The change in the unemployment rate will be .4 per cent, and the NDP says no. They want more unemployment now to protect tomorrow's prosperity, so they say. The approximate average per year balance of payments will be improved by $2 billion.
Potential Canadian content, something the NDP was very worried about when we had the debate on the bill in 1978, is 90 per cent, and they say they want to help Canadian industry. They do not want to help Canadian industry. All they want to do is to bring forward their doctrine and their dogma. They think they have an issue here with which they can fool the Canadian people, but the Canadian people will not be fooled by the bombastic NDP. There will be Canadian manufacturing benefits of $750 million. There will be Canadian manufacturing expenditures of $400 million. There will be plant expansion of $365 million. There will be research and development amounting to $35 million.
I do not mind staying here a little longer and discussing this because the NDP will be laughed at by the country. I do not mind staying here. I do not mind coming back this week or next week, because if that is all the NDP is going to bring forward as its position, its members will be laughed at. The NDP could tell it all to us now, but its members do not have much to tell. They can be bombastic about everything this evening and keep us here all this week. That does not mean very much, so under Standing Order 6(5)(a) 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr):
That the House continue to sit this day beyond the ordinary time of daily adjournment in order to complete its consideration of the motion of the President of the Privy Council now under consideration, including any amendment or amendments proposed thereto.
July 21, 1980

Mr. Speaker, I would like to have the opportunity of getting into the debate on the pipeline question, and if 1 have time tonight, 1 intend to do so, but I would also like to speak, because we are basically on the adjournment question, about another matter first.
Certainly during this session charges and countercharges have been hurled back and forth in this House, and in the press, especially between two successors of mine, the attorney general and solicitor general of Ontario and the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kaplan), respecting the evidence and testimony taken before the McDonald royal commission relating to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police activity known as Operation Checkmate of the early 1970s.
It is not my intention to deal in any way with the actual evidence which came before the commission relating to Checkmate in either its public or its private sessions, except to say that obviously if the various alleged acts of the police had been committed by anyone other than police officers in the line of duty and the evidence had been brought to the attention of the proper law officers of the Crown, charges would certainly have been laid by now.
As solicitor general of Canada in the Clark administration, my interest was whetted by some newspaper reports of what the royal commission had heard. Therefore, on taking office 1 asked for a series of briefings on what evidence had been heard and what was still to be heard. Due to time strictures, those briefings were not completed by the time I left office, but I did have a partial report on Checkmate. To put it mildly, 1 was more than surprised and angered. That partial report was presented to me in late October just before the then minister of justice, Senator Jacques Flynn, and 1 jointly convened a federal-provincial meeting of ministers of justice, ministers of correctional institutions, attorneys general and solicitors general of all the provinces. Indeed it was the first time that all provincial and federal law officers of the Crown had been together in a single federal-provincial conference.
I must say that I was deeply concerned then, as 1 am still deeply concerned, that my provincial colleagues did not know the full story nor have the full facts on those operations.
Why, one might ask, is it any business of any provincial minister what a federal police force does or what happens before a federal royal commission? It is simply this: in my view a provincial attorney general under our constitution is the
Summer Recess
chief law officer of the Crown charged with the administration of justice for that province and is almost exclusively responsible for bringing to justice anyone, anyone who commits a criminal act in that province. This is very clearly a provincial responsibility. I am also old-fashioned enough to believe that it is the duty of any citizen, no matter what his rank and position, whether he is a royal commissioner, a judge sitting in any capacity, a prime minister, a minister of justice or any other officer of the court or of the Crown, and certainly any solicitor general or any policeman or peace officer, to lay before the proper officials any evidence they may have about anything which could in any way be illegal and certainly any facts or circumstances which could involve criminal activity. Those facts should be given as soon as possible to the person or his agent who is charged with enforcing the Criminal Code in the courts. In this country, that person is the provincial attorney general. In my mind the facts in operation Checkmate indicated to me that at least four provincial attorneys general should have been informed long before I came on to the scene of the evidence that either had been or was about to be presented to that royal commission.
Members should appreciate as well that in most instances a curious solicitor general can find out in advance what is going to be presented to that particular royal commission, because the source for almost all the information that goes to the McDonald royal commission is either RCMP files or testimony from RCMP personnel or ex-personnel. If the facts known to the RCMP were transmitted to my provincial colleagues, as I think they should have been, it then would have been their job and it would be within their discretion to decide what to do with them. That is their responsibility. It is not left to the discretion of the federal Solicitor General, it is not left to the discretion of the federal Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), it is not left to the discretion of the royal commission, but it is at the discretion and the responsibility of provincial attorneys general to decide to prosecute or not to do so.
Ideally that information, with sworn statements naming names, dates and location, all available to the federal solicitor general, should have been collected, collated, and because of the belief that criminal acts had been committed, should have been sent to the provincial attorneys general. The reasons why I was unable to transmit that information to my provincial colleagues in October were fourfold. First, not all of the facts known to the RCMP had been presented to the royal commission. Second, because the commission itself had not completed taking testimony on Checkmate, as I indicated, further acts, or indeed extenuating circumstances, might still be presented to the commission, and therefore, either or both the royal commission or the provincial attorneys general might end up with information denied the other. Third, we were about to convene a federal-provincial conference when the matter could be discussed. Finally, the complete transcripts of the royal commission relating to Checkmate were not available, obviously, because the testimony was not completed. It was the transcripts, not the solicitor general's versions of the facts, that the provincial attorneys general wanted.

July 21, 1980
Summer Recess
At the federal-provincial meeting at the end of October, to the surprise of some federal officials, but on behalf of the federal government, 1 gave to the provincial attorneys general what 1 thought was an ironclad commitment, to use a hackneyed phrase around here, that as soon as the Checkmate testimony before the royal commission was completed and the transcripts made available, the uncensored, unedited testimony, along with any other evidence, knowledge or facts pertaining to those occurrences in the RCMP files or within the knowledge of the solicitor general, would be turned over to the provincial attorneys general, in advance of any public disclosure of the testimony, so that my provincial colleagues could perform their constitutional responsibilities before the courts and under the criminal law, and also from a practical point of view and for the sake of courtesy, so that they could have a reasoned response once the fat hit the fan. The attorneys general were appreciative. I think they left that conference last October secure, having received the commitment 1 had given them on behalf of the federal government.
Some time around the end of the year I was informed that all the testimony and evidence relating to Checkmate was in and that the royal commission had moved on to other matters. As far as 1 am aware, the Checkmate occurrences were the only, if not the main, allegations of potential illegalities by the RCMP outlined to the royal commission in the period between June 4 and December 12 when the Clark government fell, and therefore comprised the only testimony and allegations that 1 felt I could transmit at that time to the provincial officers of the Crown.
As we all know, on December 13, the government was plunged into a general election. The full transcripts were not received by me before then, or indeed since then. During the election campaign, I believe some time early in January, I was surprised to learn from my departmental official that within a few days, but certainly before the end of January, edited and censored versions of the McDonald transcripts were to be released to the public by the commission, edited and censored, 1 may add, not by the government, not by the Solicitor General, but by the McDonald commission itself.
I was truly incensed. My officials knew, but perhaps did not approve, of my commitment; the royal commission knew of my commitment, although they might not have agreed with it; and certainly the provinces knew of my commitment, and that I intended to live up to that commitment. The relationship between a minister of the Crown and a royal commission is hazy, to say the least. I had no means of enforcing any order, desire or command 1 might want to issue to the commission, and in any event unlike prior solicitors general I had attempted to establish a pretty good relationship with that particular commission. But I certainly did not want those transcripts released until the provinces received them first. If anyone was going to vet anything from a security point of view, that was my job as a minister primarily responsible for national security and not theirs. I strongly believed that as with the commission's first report I would probably have been willing to release the whole testimony, unedited and uncut, to the attorneys
general and to trust their judgment which, quite frankly, 1 am sure is as good as my own and certainly as good as that of any royal commission, confident that matters affecting national security, civil rights or individual privacy would be respected by them-and by "them" I mean the provincial attorneys general.
At my insistence, and I had to insist, the edited versions were therefore not released in January. The whole matter was put off until after the February election at which time, once re-elected and reappointed as solicitor general, 1 had determined to make sure that the provincial attorneys general had all of the information, not just the information the royal commission thought they should have or just the information that a federal solicitor general thought they should have. Well, as you know, Mr. Speaker, we did not win and I was not the solicitor general any longer. I noted with interest that within hours of the change of government severely edited and censored versions of those transcripts were released to the public by the commission and to this day, in defiance of the commitment given by me in good faith on behalf of the federal government, the provincial attorneys general as the proper officers of the Crown have not yet received the full facts or the full, unedited, uncut, uncensored transcripts or any of the facts or evidence contained in the RCMP files on this matter. I can only term this a very real dereliction of duty on the part of the present Solicitor General of Canada and I consider it a very real abuse of the system of Canadian justice and a continuing blow to the reputation, spirit and morale of the members of the RCMP who would, I am sure, whether they are implicated or not, want to get the whole thing over with.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few brief words on the pipeline question. Our policy in the Conservative party has been consistent throughout. Unlike the Liberals, unlike the NDP, our position throughout on this matter, going right back to the time of the original concept of the northern pipeline to take Alaskan or northern gas down through to the states or the southern part of Canada, has been consistent. Sir, we want the full, whole, complete northern pipeline.
Hear, hear!

There is no question about that. It will provide jobs, it will provide investment capital. It will put a spark to the Canadian economy that it badly needs today. It is a facility which can help enormously to develop Canada's northern potential and help solve some of North America's energy problems.
The question before the House comes down to this: What can we do to encourage the building of the pipeline? There are those who state that by going ahead and building the lower portion only, we are removing the incentive to build the line as a whole. This is obviously the view of the New Democratic Party and they are entitled to that view. They may be wrong, but they are entitled to hold that opinion. The government's view is that at a time of economic recession, construction of
July 21, 1980

the pipeline will provide the revenue, the experience, the technology and the expertise needed to move ahead with the whole line at a later date.
Speaking only for myself, I must confess that I am not happy with either position. 1 just wish there was a more recognizable thrust or anxiety on the part of the Liberals to make sure that the whole line is built. I hope we are not being "conned". I think, quite frankly, that the arm of the United States could have been twisted harder, that public and private pressures could have been exerted to obtain those "ironclad" guarantees the minister used to huff and puff about. But the Liberals have not done this. We have no guarantees and, frankly, this worries me. The government, with all the information it now possesses, obviously feels we should go ahead with the pre-build now and with construction of the whole line afterwards. So be it. 1 am willing to give them the benefit of the doubt. If that is their policy, we agree to go along with them after earnest consideration. Indeed, I think the mass of the Canadian people is willing to go along with the government's policy now. In deciding upon this procedure, the government is in possession of information which is, perhaps, not available to us. Very well. But the die is cast. The ball is in the government's court. The pre-build will go ahead in accordance with the government's decision. But 1 say this by way of warning to members opposite: If, by any chance, the rest of it, the whole of the northern portion, is not started by the end of 1983, then, to put it mildly, all hell is going to break loose. We will go along with the pre-build scheme only because it is apparent the government has decided that this is the best way to get the whole of the line built. But if this does not happen, if they are pulling the wool over the eyes of the Canadian public, if somehow or other they have been bought, if this is a con job, then by golly, if that line is not started by the end of 1983, 1 say to them: Look out, the assurances of this government will be one of the greatest traitorous "con jobs" ever perpetrated on a trusting Canadian people.
We are going along with the government only because we feel this will be a help, not a hindrance, to the building of the whole line.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this debate. I agree with the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), when he stated that this is the single most important issue to come up at this session of Parliament, but that is where our agreement ends. He sees only the negative side, while I interpret the decision as positive.
In my short time in the House I have formed certain impressions. The role the NDP sees for itself is one of negative criticism. 1 know that our democratic system is based on criticism from the opposition. But opposition should be objectively critical and have positive alternatives to suggest. My impression is that the members opposite rarely have a positive suggestion to offer. Perhaps this is conditioned by the fact that
Summer Recess
they know they are never going to be in a position to govern and therefore need make no positive suggestions.
I submit that a good example of negative thinking was held up last week when the member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) stated that on this issue he was never so proud "as not to be a Liberal". Why wouldn't he say rather, that he was proud to be a member of the New Democratic Party? 1 think the answer is obvious. He cannot be proud to be a member of such a negative party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the members of the New Domocratic Party have been the obstructionists in the House and since they brought in the motion, will they at least follow one word in the title of their party, which is "democratic" and at least be democratic enough to let the hon. member be heard.
You were the heckler when I spoke.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext: Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we could invite you to demand order. The hon. member is a new member in the House and perhaps the NDP should show sufficient common courtesy through their leader to at least allow the hon. member to be heard. Since they do want to hold up Parliament and hold up the country, and since they do want to create unemployment in this country and since they do want to be absolutely opposed to what they are supposed to stand for, I think they should at least be democratic enough to let the hon. member be heard.
Listen to who is talking about being democratic.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to be a Liberal. I am proud to be a member of a party which has men of the calibre of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) who are showing great leadership in this Alaska gas pipeline solution. 1 am proud to be a member of a party which recognizes the importance of jobs which will be created by the immediate construction of the pre-build pipeline.
I am pleased that the community of Hamilton and other neighbouring cities to my constituency will be the major beneficiaries. As a result of the help which this project will be to the steel industry, 1 know that the effect will ripple into my own constituency. Also, on the positive side, there will be new jobs created. This is vastly in contrast to the negative attitude of the NDP, who would rather preserve their right to think they are right than to support a project which would create jobs which we need right now.
I am proud because we are giving encouragement to those people in western Canada who have faith in our economy and our country. As private entrepreneurs, they have found gas in abundance and can now market that gas and begin to get a return on their investment, thus creating the possibility for them to stay in Canada as viable Canadian companies and to have the capital resources to further their successes by finding more oil and gas. This will ultimately help to ensure our energy independence.

July 21, 1980
Summer Recess
While being sensibly responsive to the need of assurance about the intention of the United States to keep their part of the bargain, we recognize the natural market for our gas. We are aware of the need our neighbour has for this gas and we are willing to share what we have in abundance. Energy disruptions in the U.S.A. are at the heart of American economic problems. It is clearly in our best interest to assist our best ally when it has a need.
I am sure hon. members have heard the quotation "When the United States catches a cold, we in Canada catch pneumonia". Political realism makes it necessary for all countries to be careful and vigilant with respect to agreements and promises. 1 believe that while we may sometimes lose faith in politicians and governments, we must never lose faith in people. For that reason our very survival dictates that we learn to share what we have. Where better to start than with our friends and neighbours? Sharing, once begun, can lead the way to a mutual sharing on this continent which can serve as a model to other parts of the world, places that do not have the basis of understanding which is natural to our two great nations.
I am positive about this pipeline. 1 base my evidence not on the past and not on past decisions, but on the evidence which 1 see now. There is such evidence as even according to the NEB, the volume of Canadian gas that is surplus to our needs and available for export has grown from some 800 billion cubic feet to around 4.5 trillion cubic feet. 1 am impressed by the fact that the United States has said that it has an absolutely vital national interest in securing access to its gas in Prudhoe Bay in Alaska because it represents more than 10 per cent of its total reserves. Tapping these reserves is essential to the United States for security of reliable supply. 1 am impressed because, according to Foothills' calculations, pre-building would lead to direct capital expenditures in Canada of some $1.6 billion-$665 million on the pipeline itself and a further $935 million on associated gas production, conditioning and gathering facilities. Together these outlays would provided an estimated 150,000 man years of employment between 1980 and 1984. These are jobs. I am impressed by the fact that, given the nature of the U.S. assurances, the government has decided that there is minimal risk of non-completion or long delay in the construction of the entire Alaska gas pipeline.
On the other hand, there are substantial benefits which pre-building will provide. Facility and completion of the entire project will bring immediate returns to Canada in terms of jobs, output of producer revenues and balance of payment influences. I do not believe that there can be any doubt that our natural interest lies in proceeding with this important undertaking at the earliest possible date. My mind is made up and convinced by the facts. Do not try to confuse me with fiction.
In contrast, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) in no way answered the question with facts, but instead tried to throw up a smoke screen to cover the fact that this party's position will not lose jobs for his riding. He talks about
somebody being phony. Since he brought out the facts, he just confirmed that what he wants to do to the workers in his constituency is what Masters and Johnson is all about.
New jobs are important, the development of industry is important, and the encouragement of Canadian-owned resource development is important. 1 am convinced that the pipeline should be built now by Canadians for Canadians because in the end it will be Canadians who benefit most from this imaginative project.
Mr. Speaker, may 1 call it ten o'clock?

cratic Party, but a limited debate nonetheless. There is no question of spending the whole summer in this House to please 30 members out of 282.
