speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: ENERGY-EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS TO UNITED STATES
ENERGY-EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question 1 want to raise this evening is relevant to some of the matters that have been discussed today. Indeed, it is rather coincidental.
On April 17, the second day of this sitting, I directed a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) asking whether he maintained the position he took on December 6 last in opposition to the export of natural gas to the United States. I also inquired, in the course of my questioning, about the minister's policy with respect to natural gas and whether he had made a statement that one of his priorities would be to introduce an export tax on natural gas. I also asked him whether, if that was a statement of government policy, it continued to be so.
In response, the minister gave a rather unsatisfactory and vague statement to the effect that the government was looking into the matter. Subsequent to that date, we have had a statement by the minister with respect to the Alaska natural gas pipeline, but we still have not heard from him, by way of a
Adjournment Debate
policy statement on the question of an export tax on natural gas.
I think it would be useful to look back at what was said on December 6 and put on the record again exactly what the minister said at that time when he was the Liberal party critic on energy matters.
1 quote from page 2101 of Hansard for December 6. At that time the minister said:
In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all, an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline. Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered, particularly the financing plan and the financing guarantees, before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.
We have had the statement with respect to the assurances of the completion of the total project. But the second interesting ironclad requirement which the minister indicated at that time was as follows:
Second, there must be an arrangement for swaps in this agreement with the United States so that down the line, if Canada were to need natural gas, we would be in a position to obtain natural gas from the Alaska gas pipeline which we might need in exchange for the gas we are now providing to the Americans. That would be the second point.
The minister continued by saying:
The third point is with regard to revenues arising out of gas exports to the United States. They should be used to ensure the initiation and completion of the Quebec and maritime gas pipeline so that eastern Canada would be fully served in terms of gas service and so that people in the maritimes and eastern Quebec would be assured of getting natural gas at a reasonable price.
There you have, Mr. Speaker, what I consider to be some fairly firm and unequivocal statements made by the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I would be interested in finding out on three very important points precisely whether or not he still holds that position. We have heard nothing with respect to the whole question of swaps. That was a fundamental question. We have heard nothing at all with respect to the completion of the natural gas pipeline to the maritimes which was to be financed out of the moneys to be made on the Alaska natural gas pipeline.
The third point is that we had a statement in response to my question by the minister on April 17, with respect to an export tax on natural gas. It can be found in Hansard at page 96, and it reads as follows:
Madam Speaker, I do not recall ever having made such a statement.
He goes on to say:
If the hon. member has such a quote, I would like to see it.
The important words are these:
But this is not part of government policy.
We have had innumerable reports that the minister is seriously considering an export tax on natural gas. He says now that he is considering not only natural gas but an export tax on other resources which are exported out of the country, including electricity. He has been somewhat quieter lately with respect to this proposition because he is receiving a lot of opposition on the latter proposition from the provinces of Quebec and Ontario.

July 21, 1980
Adjournment Debate
If the parliamentary secretary is going to answer for the minister tonight, 1 would like to know whether or not these items are still fundamental with respect to the Alaska natural gas pipeline, whether we can take the minister at his word- his word has been considered very leniently up to this point but we expect him to be consistent-that an export tax on natural gas is not part of government policy. I would like a clear and unequivocal statement. I would like to have that reaffirmed by the parliamentary secretary tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENERGY-EXPORT OF NATURAL GAS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond on behalf of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to the question which the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) raised on April 17. I would point out to him that it is that particular question to which I propose to respond, not the new twist which he put to it tonight relating to taxation on gas exports.
I propose responding to him on the matter of substance which he raised on that particular date because we assume full well, knowing the gentleman as we do, that that was his concern, and we shall attempt to address ourselves to that tonight.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources responded to the question raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon West last April concerning the undertaking that would be required before gas exports could be approved, the minister stated that the government at that time had decided to postpone any action concerning approval of gas exports until a clearer indication was obtained from the United States government than the previous government, led by the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), had been able to obtain with regard to the United States commitment to the Alaska pipeline project.
We have now obtained the necessary assurances, subject only to confirmation from the sponsoring pipeline group, that financing can be completed for the pre-build section and for the rest of the pipeline within Canadian territory.
As the minister stated in the House of Commons on July 17, the assurances received from the United States have been expressed in several ways. First, there were the decisions by the federal energy regulatory commission, a U.S. government agency, certifying the pre-building of the western and eastern legs of the northern pipeline system within the U.S. for the initial purpose of transporting surplus Alberta gas and for the transportation of Alaska reserves when the system is completed from Prudhoe Bay.
Second, on June 19 there was an agreement between the major gas producers in Alaska and the northwest Alaskan Pipeline on the sharing of $500 million worth of expenditures to complete the final design and engineering work that will be necessary preparatory to constructing the pipeline and the
various related facilities in Alaska. This was a clear intention of the sponsoring companies to proceed with the project.
Third, on June 19 the oil companies holding the reserves in Prudhoe Bay and the pipeline company also signed a statement of intention in which they undertook to work together to facilitate the financing of the pipeline and related facilities in Alaska with the objective of building the entire system by 1985.
Of course, there have been other assurances since then, including a resolution by the United States Congress and the letter from President Carter to which reference has been made in this House in the last few days.
Based on these formal assurances, and an assessment of the importance of the project to the Canadian economy, the Canadian government has taken the decision to proceed with the project. The widespread support of the government's decision to approve this major pipeline project, and the related gas exports, has been evident in the past few days through many messages of support from a broad spectrum throughout the Canadian economy.
And, finally, may 1 say to the hon. member, yes, you can take the minister at his word.

AIR TRANSPORT-SCHEDULED JET AIR SERVICE TO BRANDON, MAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening on behalf of many of the residents of southwestern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan who have been without air service connecting them with points east and west in Canada. Brandon services a large number of people. The city is made up of about 40,000 people. It services some 130,000 people in southwestern and western Manitoba. It has been without regular scheduled air service to points east and west for a considerable period of time.
Prior to 1969, Brandon was linked to Winnipeg and Regina by turbojet. This service was transferred to TransAir which in turn terminated flights from Brandon in 1972. Since then, the residents of Brandon and area have been effectively stranded when it comes to travelling to either Calgary or Toronto.
When a resident of the Brandon area wishes to travel either east or west, he must somehow get to Winnipeg. If he is going west, he must overfly Brandon in order to get to either Regina or Calgary. Going east, someone living in Brandon has to travel approximately 130 miles to Winnipeg, worry about parking, and board an aircraft travelling to eastern Canada.
Brandon is a very progressive area. A year ago it hosted the Canada Winter Games, and did an outstanding job. In 1982, Brandon will be hosting the Labatt's Brier, an event of national significance. A city which will be hosting that kind of event obviously must have the services available to do a proper job. The city of Brandon has approximately 1,000 hotel units. It is capable of attracting conventions. It is, from my own experience, home of one of the nicest livestock sale pavilions, and
July 21, 1980

when it comes to cattle, it has some of the best breeding stock in Canada.
It seems to me that air service into Brandon would provide an impetus to that area and link it not only with points in Canada but also points in the United States on which we depend for buyers.
Brandon is also an agricultural and a very large commercial centre. It is the centre of a large grain-growing area. The retail sales in the Brandon area in 1979 were some 30 per cent above the national average. To my mind this is all a way of saying that Brandon is a growing and energetic city which needs-in fact, deserves-the added impetus of regularly scheduled direct flights to other Canadian trade centres.
I raised this question with the minister in the House back on May 29 when I had an opportunity to ask him about this. I will eliminate some of the preamble and read into the record what 1 asked him back on May 29, as follows:
Would the minister tell the House and the people of that area what the government's position is in terms of this service, which is very much in need in that important area of Manitoba?
Among other things the minister said the following:
However, I am trying to help matters move faster.
That was nearly two months ago. We have not seen action on this since that time. In a supplementary question to the minister 1 tried to point out to him that this was an urgent matter, and he responded by saying, and I quote:
I would prefer the CTC to make an objective appraisal of the situation, knowing full well that I and the government as a whole can change that decision if judged necessary.
The implication I drew from that was that once the CTC had held hearings and if it was not satisfactory to the people of Brandon and area, the government would be willing to take another look at it. Since then, as I said, nothing has happened.
What did happen when we were the government was that back on November 21 the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), while on a trip to Brandon on which I had the pleasure to accompany him and when he was speaking to the annual convention of the Union of Manitoba Municipalities, said that he had cleared the way for regional air carriers to apply for this route. I will read part of the press release which accompanied his speech, as follows:
Without this announcement, Mr. Mazankowski said, there could otherwise have been concern that a licence application for such a service might be rejected by the Canadian Transport Commission as being incompatible with a provision in the regional air carrier policy that regional carriers should not expand as potential transcontinental operators.
By making this announcement the then minister made it possible for regional air carriers to apply for that route without violating the transportation policy of the government. It seems to me that the position of the government should be to set policy, and it should then be the position of the CTC to enforce it or see that that kind of policy is carried out. What I find unfortunate today, despite the fact that there have been 350 petitions from the area in support of that kind of service, is
Adjournment Debate
that this government has seen fit not to push the CTC to set a date for hearings. What we did have a week ago was a situation in which Frontier Airlines, a foreign air carrier based in Nevada, made an application for a route to fly into Saskatchewan to pick up passengers at Saskatoon and Regina and then to carry on to Minot and Denver. This application was made and this route was granted without a hearing. What 1 find disturbing is that in the case of our own country, the government has not even pushed the CTC enough to set hearings. The application before the CTC for this route is made by Pacific Western Airlines. It is a Canadian company which is willing to provide this service on a daily basis without a subsidy.
The air terminal at Brandon is a controlled terminal. There is a new building there. The runways are of sufficient length that the service could be commenced without any additional moneys being spent. There is a small problem. On hot days during the summer, the 737s which PWA proposes to use may not be able to take off at full load and have enough fuel to get to Toronto going east. However, in its submission to the CTC, TWA said this, concerning that rather minor problem:
Operationally, the length of this runway will occasionally impose payload restrictions on a Boeing 737 operation between Brandon and Toronto. However, on such infrequent occasions, the applicant is prepared to make an en route technical stop at Winnipeg on eastbound services between Brandon and Toronto.
We have a situation in which an area of Canada is very much in need of, and deserves, this kind of service but is without it. A Canadian air carrier has applied for this service, and we have a government which is not prepared to go ahead and see that a hearing is set so that a Canadian company can provide services for a very important area of the country. 1 urge the government to go ahead and set a date for the hearings as quickly as possible so that we can have this kind of service which is much needed and overdue in western Manitoba.

I can therefore appreciate their impatience, now that PWA has formally applied to the CTC for a licence to provide the jet services desired.
1 understand that the application was filed with the CTC on January 21 of this year. The fact that the application is still under consideration by the commission makes it inappropriate for me to comment on the case lest my comments be interpreted as prejudicial to an unbiased consideration of the matter by the CTC. All that 1 can say at the moment is that the CTC is required by law to follow certain procedures in considering applications for new air services. For example, the application must be advertised in the newspapers of the area to allow anyone interested to intervene in support of or against the application. These parties must then be given adequate time, as specified in the CTC regulations, to file their interventions,

to which the applicant is then given the opportunity to reply. In the case of the PWA application to serve Brandon and Toronto, this process was not completed until late March. ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-MOVEMENT OF OH. BY TANKER-GOVERNMENT REPRESENTATION AT U.S. HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my concern is with the proposal to have an oil tanker superport at Port Angeles, Washington. On different occasions since the February 18 election, 1 have asked different ministers about their stand on this in the House. Also I have written letters to the ministers. In neither case have 1 received satisfactory answers.
1 should like to outline briefly some of the reasons why the people in my constituency and all the people on the coast of British Columbia are so concerned about this tanker traffic. First, there is a distinct possibility-perhaps I should say a statistical inevitability-that there will be a major superspill sometime off the coast of British Columbia which will result in ecological disaster.
Dr. Andrew Thompson in his final report for the West Coast Oil Ports Inquiry said:
Time is on your side only until a spill occurs; an Amoca Cadiz could ground in Rosario Strait tomorrow.
This is a worldwide problem. Between 1969 and 1973, a total of 82 losses occurred. There were hundreds of other minor mishaps in which a great deal of oil was spilled.
Second, we are concerned about the incremental damage which will come through small spills, through seepage from hook-ups, and from illegal flushing. In many areas, this incremental damage is even more serious than the threat of one major spill, because this is something which is going on day after day, week after week, year after year. It is destructive of marine life.
Third, there is the danger to fishing vessels and other small craft in the shipping lanes. There are numerous instances, in areas where there is tanker traffic, of trawlers and other fishing vessels just mysteriously disappearing. We do not need to have a Bermuda Triangle to explain that sort of thing. In many cases they have simply been hit by supertankers which did not even know they hit these vessels. They just kept going and lives have been lost. I do not want to see that kind of situation prevailing off the coast of British Columbia.
Finally, the presence of a major tanker terminal less than 20 miles from the city of Victoria could create a serious air pollution problem. In his statement of proceedings before the West Coast Oil Ports Inquiry, Dr. Thompson talked about this aspect and said:
It is possible that the emissions from the tankers, docks and storage tanks mixed with the air pollution from the existing forest industry operations at Port Angeles would exceed established standards with such frequency as to place in question the continuing viability of the oil port operations. If authorities enforce air quality standards by closing down offloading operations when violations occur, the resultant queuing of tankers in the Strait of Juan de Fuca could seriously heighten navigation and oil spill risks.
For these reasons and others we are very concerned about this proposal. The government claims to be aware of these facts and has declared its opposition to a superport, but when asked specific questions about the manner in which they are expressing their opposition, when asked what they are doing, they are entirely too casual. For example, in response to my question on April 28, 1980, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) refused to have Canadian representatives present at the environmental hearings held in the State of Washington at its capital in Olympia. He had no answer to give to my request that the Department of the Environment should be conducting independent studies in this area. Two years ago, Dr. Thompson put his finger on the problem. He said:
The public concern in British Columbia is that these negotiations are not being given the priority they deserve.
Liberal policy seems to be best summed up in the phrase "Leave it alone; maybe it will go away, perhaps after the presidential election in November." As I say, the attitude of the government is entirely too casual. For instance, when asked about a Canadian presence at the site hearings in Seattle, the minister said:
The consulate general ... is keeping us fully informed of events and allowing us to assess continually the situation.
I had a similar response from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan), but when I asked him in committee to give us an update, he could not do so. I do not expect the minister to be in possession of detailed information on every subject under the sun, but we in British Columbia think this is an important subject, a priority, and that we should at least know what is happening.
So my question is this: What co-ordination is there between the various ministers involved? Who is really in charge here and what is the Department of the Environment doing to help face this threat?

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-MOVEMENT OF OH. BY TANKER-GOVERNMENT REPRESENTATION AT U.S. HEARINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, let me thank the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) for raising this important issue and pursuing it on a number of
July 21, 1980

occasions. I want to assure him on a personal basis that it is a matter of some concern to me. It is only a year or so ago, April, 1979, 1 believe, that the Kurdistan broke up off the Atlantic coast. One of the results was that several hundreds of fishermen in my own riding of Burin-St. George's found their activities disrupted; they were subsequently compensated for loss of gear but in other ways they were seriously inconvenienced. I fear that should another spill come, it might well involve more than temporary inconvenience or interruption of income. For this reason alone I share the concerns he has raised.
The hon. member said he has not been receiving satisfactory answers. 1 am not sure that what 1 have to say tonight will satisfy him either, though I believe it will satisfy a number of people who may have occasion to hear it.
For this reason, and with the strong support of the government of British Columbia, the Canadian government has publicly expressed its concern about, and opposition to, increasing tanker traffic on the west coast. We have repeatedly made our feelings known to the United States on this matter. For example, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) personally made his position clear to the United States secretary of the interior when he visited Washington back in April. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) stated this position to the energy secretary of the United States, Mr. Duncan, when he visited Ottawa last March. Even since then, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan) underlined our concerns again during the visit to Ottawa of the former United States secretary of state, Cyrus Vance.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Northern Tier Pipeline for which President Carter has expressed a preference, would be located totally within the United States. Tankers may, if necessary, proceed to and from the proposed oil port at Port Angeles entirely in the United States and international waters.
Adjournment Debate
Hearings under the Washington state permitting process with respect to the Northern Tier proposal are under way and are expected to continue until late this year with a state decision unlikely before the end of 1980. These hearings are long and involved but officials of the Department of the Environment and External Affairs are following them closely. Contrary to the statement made by the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands, we are sending specialists to the hearings as it becomes necessary.
1 can assure the hon. member and this House that the government is continuing to do everything possible to discourage additional tanker traffic on the west coast. We have also made a number of co-operative arrangements with the United States to reduce the risk to the citizens of the west coast from existing tanker traffic. For example, the provision for compensation for Canadians in the event of a spill of Alaska oil, scientific research into the marine environment and the impact of oil spills, the development of a joint oil spill contingency plan and the installation of sophisticated navigation and traffic management systems are all efforts to reduce the risk.
Finally, we recently signed a vessel traffic management agreement with the United States which, when fully implemented, will provide the Juan de Fuca region with one of the best systems of marine safety found anywhere. While we can never entirely eliminate the risk of an oil spill, we are at least working to increase the odds against it and to minimize the possibility of serious environmental damage.
I would suggest to the hon. member that the examples which 1 have given with regard to the situation can hardly be, "leaving the situation alone", as he phrased it. We are very much on top of the situation and we are conscious, as he is, of the seriousness and magnitude of the problem. We pledge to continue working on these problems.
